summary: A 1970 note by E. Meyer pointing out an error in the Logger Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 79 points out that a logger protocol proposal sends an allocation command before a connection is open. The existing NCP protocol allows that command only after opening the connection, so the author recommends changing the logger proposal.

questions: what was the logger protocol error
when could the all command be sent
how did rfc 79 recommend resolving the conflict
subtitle: A note identifying a conflict between the logger proposal and the NCP protocol.

tldr.problem: The logger protocol proposal calls for an ALL command during connection setup, while the official NCP protocol permits ALL only on an open connection.
tldr.mechanism: Edwin Meyer describes the conflict and recommends changing the proposed logger protocol to match the existing NCP restriction.
tldr.outcome: The RFC argues against changing the NCP protocol except for critical reasons, to preserve a simplifying restriction used by implementations.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 79 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The note identifies a conflict and recommends modifying the proposed logger protocol to match the existing NCP protocol.

sections.title: The Connection-Setup Conflict
sections.content:
The note identifies a conflict between the official NCP protocol in Protocol Document 1 and the logger protocol described in RFC 66. RFC 66 proposes sending an ALL allocation command immediately after an RTS or STR connection request.

Protocol Document 1 restricts the ALL command to a connection that is already open.
sections.plainLanguage: The logger proposal sends ALL while a connection is still being set up. The NCP rules described in Protocol Document 1 allow ALL only after the connection is open.

sections.title: Why the Restriction Helps Implementers
sections.content:
The note says that not having to handle ALL before a connection is established is a simplifying restriction for an NCP implementation. It gives the Multics NCP as an example of an implementation designed with this restriction.

Changing the NCP protocol would affect implementations that rely on the existing rule.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations can be simpler if they handle ALL only after a connection is open. The note says the Multics NCP was designed with that restriction.

sections.title: Change the Logger Proposal
sections.content: The author argues that the logger protocol should be modified to agree with the existing NCP protocol. He also says the NCP protocol should not be changed at that time except for critical reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: The recommended fix is to change the logger proposal so it follows the existing NCP rule. The note does not recommend changing the NCP protocol for this issue.

references.text: Crocker, S., "3rd Level Ideas and Other Noise", RFC 66, August 1970.
